projects.name: Geomagnetic Travellogue
projects.write_up:
This project follows the zero-degree line of the
earth's magnetic field from the year 1590.
It is a work in progress.

The year 1590 is significant, as it coincides with the
development of Galileo's first telescope, and with the
creation of the first compound microscope.

Therefore, my project explores incidences of macro-
and micro-scopic vision, magnetic attraction and
polarity, and the intersection of scientific, historical,
and artistic narratives.

On May 10, 2008 I made my first journey. I would attempt to go to Peru, Iceland, South Africa, and Australia.

I started my expedition in Los Angeles, and after carefully studying my maps, I plotted my destinations. I had 24 hours to make this trip.

*parallel worlds*
*using the wrong map to get to the right places*
*can I reach Peru through a looking glass?*
projects.synopsis: Tracing the zero-degree line of the earth's magnetic field from 1590 to the present, in four journeys.

children.name: Los Angeles
children.write_up:
I consider Los Angeles to be the starting and ending point for this journey. It is my birthplace, and I have lived here for 36 years.

California is known for its earthquakes, and Los Angeles sits upon the San Andreas Fault. This important faultline is where the Pacific tectonic plate slides past the North American tectonic plate. Half of Los Angeles is moving slowly towards Anchorage, Alaska. The other half is travelling south.

Los Angeles is home to Caltech, one of the foremost institutions in the study of seismic and geomagnetic activity, as well as astronomy and physics. Los Angeles is also home to the historical Mount Wilson Observatory, which is situated directly above my childhood home in Pasadena. This is where Edwin Hubble made many of his notable observations with the now antiquated 100-inch Hooker Telescope.
children.synopsis: Birthplace and fault line — Los Angeles as the start and end of the journey.

children.name: Cyprus
children.write_up:
The Mediterranean island of Cyprus has been inhabited since Neolithic times. The Greeks and the Turks have been fighting over the island for thousands of years. Ironically, it is the legendary birthplace of the Greek goddess of love, Aphrodite. The name "Cyprus" is probably a derivative of the Greek word for copper, which has been mined on the island since ancient times. This is probably the reason why Aphrodite/Venus is associated with the element copper.

It was not until November 1, 1974 (the exact day and year I was born) that a delicate peace agreement was reached for Cyprus. On this date, the U.N. drew a "green line" down the middle of the island, dividing it between the Greeks and the Turks.

I felt a certain "geomagnetic attraction" to Cyprus — from the birthday connection with this date in Cypriot history, to the mythological, anthropological, and even geological history of the place. I found the association with a "love goddess" intriguing, as well as the importance of materials like copper and honey.
children.synopsis: A birthday shared with a divided island's peace agreement, and the myths that followed.

children.name: On Slowness
children.write_up: A short entry on why the January Jones paintings took a full year to finish.
children.writing:
The paintings in this room took longer than any I have made. Not because the surfaces are complicated — most of them are just a table, a window, a fall of light — but because I kept waiting for the room to tell me it was finished, and it never quite did.

I have started to think of slowness as a material, the way I think about oil or graphite. It has a texture. It resists you in a specific way. You can push against it, and sometimes it gives, and sometimes it pushes back harder, and either way you learn something about the painting you would not have learned by finishing it quickly.

I don't think fast work is worse. I think I am just not very good at it, and I have decided to stop apologizing for that.

children.name: Studio Notes, Winter
children.write_up: Notes kept during the coldest weeks of the January Jones series.
children.writing:
The radiator in the studio makes a sound like a held breath being let go, on and off, all day. I have started timing my brushstrokes to it without meaning to.

Some days the light comes in flat and grey and every color on the palette looks like a compromise. Other days, for maybe twenty minutes around four in the afternoon, the whole room goes the color of a bruise healing, and I try to work fast enough to catch it before it changes. I rarely do. That failure is most of what this series is about.

children.name: Working Method
children.write_up: How the studies for Frost Line led to the finished painting.
children.writing:
I usually draw a room four or five times before I let myself paint it. The drawings are not preparatory in the usual sense — I'm not solving composition problems, I already know where the table goes. I'm trying to memorize the room well enough that I can paint it later without needing to look at it, the way you might learn a piece of music well enough to play it with your eyes closed.

By the time I started Frost Line, I had drawn that corner of the studio often enough that I painted most of it from memory, checking the actual room only twice, both times to confirm something about the color of the frost on the glass rather than its shape.

items.name: Correspondence with a Painter I Never Met
items.write_up: An essay written after finding a box of unsent letters at an estate sale.
items.writing:
I bought the letters for four dollars, in a shoebox that also held a broken thermometer and a lot of loose buttons. They were addressed to no one in particular — drafts, it seems, rather than letters that were ever sent — and they were all about painting, in the specific, granular way that people only write when they don't expect to be read.

I don't know the writer's name. I know she worked in a cold room, that she distrusted her own blues, and that she once spent three weeks on a single square foot of a canvas she eventually painted over entirely. I think about her more than I think about painters I actually know, possibly because there is nothing left to argue with. She only gets to be right.
